sec: Transaminitis patterns · acute vs chronic, alcoholic ratios and non-hepatic causes

items.q: Severe acute elevations of serum transaminases (>1000 U/L) are typically seen in viral, toxic, and ischemic hepatitis, but can also occur acutely in which biliary emergency?
items.exp: The margin note highlights: 'Severe acute elevations also seen in Acute bile duct obstruction (>1000 U/L).' (Book p989)

items.q: Match each viral cause of acute hepatitis with its most common demographic group — 1) Hepatitis A virus (HAV) 2) Hepatitis E virus (HEV) … A) Most common in adults B) Most common in children
items.exp: HAV is noted as most common in children, whereas HEV is noted as most common in adults. (Book p989)

items.q: What is the typical transaminase level and AST:ALT ratio seen in uncomplicated alcoholic hepatitis?
items.exp: Alcoholic liver disease characteristically presents with transaminase values of 300–500 U/L and an AST > ALT pattern. (Book p989)

items.q: A 42-year-old chronic alcohol consumer presents with right upper quadrant pain and jaundice. His AST is 380 U/L and ALT is 120 U/L (ratio > 3:1). Why is AST higher than ALT in alcoholic liver disease?
opts: ALT synthesis requires greater amounts of pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), which is deficient in alcoholics
Ethanol directly stimulates mitochondrial AST transcription in zone 1 hepatocytes
ALT is rapidly cleared by hepatic reticuloendothelial cells during ethanol exposure
Alcohol causes selective transcriptional suppression of the cytoplasmic ALT gene
items.exp: AST exceeds ALT in alcoholic liver disease because ALT requires more pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), which is depleted in chronic alcoholics. (Book p989)

items.q: Match each AST:ALT ratio threshold with its diagnostic interpretation in alcoholic liver injury — 1) AST:ALT >= 2:1 2) AST:ALT >= 3:1 … A) Definitive alcoholic hepatitis B) Almost always alcoholic hepatitis
items.exp: An AST:ALT ratio of 2:1 is 'almost always alcoholic hepatitis', while a ratio of 3:1 is 'definitive alcoholic hepatitis'. (Book p989)

items.q: A patient with established alcoholic cirrhosis presents after a heavy drinking binge with severe acute jaundice and transaminases exceeding 1000 U/L with AST > ALT. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: Values >1000 U/L with AST > ALT indicate acute-on-chronic alcoholic liver disease. (Book p989)

items.q: What numeric threshold defines mild transaminase elevation in chronic hepatitis?
opts: < 5 times the upper limit of normal or < 150 U/L
< 2 times the upper limit of normal or < 60 U/L
< 10 times the upper limit of normal or < 300 U/L
< 20 times the upper limit of normal or < 500 U/L
items.exp: Mild transaminase elevation in chronic hepatitis is defined as < 5 times upper limit of normal or < 150 U/L. (Book p989)

items.q: Which of the following conditions causes mild transaminase elevation (<150 U/L) with AST > ALT rather than ALT > AST?
items.exp: Cirrhosis and hypothyroidism produce an AST > ALT pattern; Wilson's disease, hemochromatosis, celiac disease, HBV, HCV, and autoimmune hepatitis show ALT > AST. (Book p989)

items.q: Why does cirrhosis result in an inverted AST > ALT pattern in chronic liver disease?
opts: Decreased sinusoidal uptake and clearance of AST by damaged liver tissue
Induction of mitochondrial enzyme release from regenerating nodules
Selective renal retention of AST over ALT
Preferential biliary excretion of ALT over AST
items.exp: In cirrhosis, an AST > ALT pattern arises from decreased sinusoidal uptake of AST by the cirrhotic liver. (Book p989)

items.q: A 58-year-old man presents with chest tightness and diaphoresis. An LFT panel shows normal ALT (22 U/L) but markedly elevated AST (420 U/L). What is the most appropriate deduction?
opts: The enzyme elevation is of non-hepatic origin, such as myocardial infarction or rhabdomyolysis
The patient has acute classic viral hepatitis A infection
The patient has decompensated cirrhosis with portal hypertension
The patient has acute ischemic shock liver
items.exp: Isolated AST elevation with normal ALT points to a non-hepatic origin such as myocardial infarction or rhabdomyolysis. (Book p989)

items.q: Assess the two statements: I A rising serum bilirubin accompanied by a falling AST/ALT always indicates complete hepatocellular recovery. II Reduced viable hepatocyte mass in diabetic steatohepatitis (NASH) can cause transaminases to appear falsely modest despite progressive damage.
items.exp: Statement I is false because rising bilirubin with falling AST/ALT does not correlate with recovery; it can indicate loss of viable hepatocytes. Statement II is true as noted for DM/NASH. (Book p989)

items.q: Fill up: In a patient with chronic hepatitis, the presence of cirrhosis as the cause of an AST > ALT pattern is typically confirmed or ruled out non-invasively by ______.
items.exp: The diagram indicates that cirrhosis under the AST > ALT branch is '(Ruled out by fibro scan)'. (Book p989)
